briefdescription.para: The Node.js back-end of the CloudAvid File Portal: a zero-framework HTTP server that serves the SPA shell, static assets, a filesystem-driven JSON API, and streamed downloads.

sect2.title: 🧒 ELI5 Summary
sect2.para: Think of this file as the reception desk of a building.

You (the browser) walk in the front door and say things like: "I want the welcome brochure" (the index.html page), or "Can I see the list of rooms?" (/api/categories), or "Please hand me the big box in room 3, shelf 2" (/api/download/...). The receptionist — this file — never builds the rooms itself and never touches the boxes directly. It just listens to what you ask for, checks that you are allowed to have it, and then calls the right specialist (the modules in lib/) who does the actual walking-and-fetching. If you ask for something dangerous — like "give me the staff-only key cabinet" (/lib/, /.env) — the receptionist politely but firmly says "403 Forbidden" and does not even look inside.

listitem.para: HTTP Endpoint: Creates the single Node.js http.Server for the whole project and binds it to 0.0.0.0 on the configured port. It is the only network listener in the repository.
Environment Bootstrap: Loads process.env from the project-root .env file (via lib/load-env.js) before anything else reads it.
JSON API Router: Implements six API endpoints (/api/health, /api/categories, /api/releases, /api/search, /api/files, /api/download) by delegating all filesystem work to lib/files-service.js.
SPA Fallback Server: Returns index.html for /, /browse, and any unknown HTML-ish route, so client-side routing (assets/js/router.js) works on refresh and deep links.
Static Asset Server: Serves assets/, fonts, icons and other files from the project root with a curated MIME table, a one-hour cache policy, and an inline SVG placeholder for missing images.

Security Gatekeeper: Blocks path traversal, blocks access to /.env, /lib/, /node_modules/, sets nosniff / SAMEORIGIN / strict-origin-when-cross-origin headers on every served response, and sanitises the Content-Disposition filename of downloads.

Cross-Origin Enabler: Answers CORS preflights (OPTIONS) and stamps Access-Control-Allow-Origin: * on every JSON and download response, because nginx.conf proxies only the /api/ prefix and other origins may call the API directly.
Ops Surface: Colour-coded request logging, a startup banner that reports the health of FILES_ROOT, a health endpoint for uptime monitors, and a graceful SIGINT shutdown handler.

sect2.title: 🧭 Role in the Overall Architecture
sect2.para: server.js is the front door of the back-end. It contains zero filesystem logic of its own; every read, stat, walk and safety check on the downloads tree is delegated to lib/files-service.js. This is a deliberate two-layer split:

listitem.para: server.js = transport layer (HTTP, headers, streaming, CORS, routing).
lib/files-service.js = domain layer (FILES_ROOT resolution, path sanitisation, directory walking, search, release ranking).

sect2.para: The frontend mirror of this split is assets/js/services/resource-service.js, which is the only frontend file allowed to call this server's API.

sect1.title: 🏗️ Architecture: How A Request Flows Through This File
sect1.para: The diagram below shows every decision point of the main request handler. Note the deliberate ordering: URL parse → CORS preflight → method filter → security blocklist → API routes → SPA routes → static fallback → error net.

The dependency graph below shows how server.js connects the whole project: it consumes the environment layer, delegates the domain work, and is consumed by nginx (in production), npm start (in development), and the frontend's single API client.

sect1.title: 🧩 File Header Comment
sect1.para:
📍 Location
The very first lines of server.js.
🎯 Purpose (ELI5)
This is the name-tag on the reception desk. It tells a human skimming the repository what this file is and on which operating systems it runs. It carries no executable meaning — it is purely documentation inside code.
🔗 Trace Downward
Pure comment; no runtime effect. The claims it makes ("filesystem-driven", "Windows + Linux") are backed by lib/files-service.js (which normalises separators with path.* calls) and by this file's path.join / path.normalize usage throughout.
🤝 Trace Sideways
The ═══ banner style is the project's house convention for module headers; the same style opens lib/files-service.js... and, on the frontend, assets/js/resource-service.js, assets/js/router.js and assets/js/autocomplete.js.
💻 Actual Code
/*═══════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════ server.js—CloudAvidFilePortal Filesystem-drivenHTTPserver(Windows+Linux) ═══════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════*/
When editing, keep this banner comment syntactically closed. If the closing delimiter (* immediately followed by /) is lost, the require("http") below it becomes part of the comment and the server crashes on startup with http is not defined.
─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────

sect1.title: 🧩 Block: Core Module Requires (http, fs, path, URL)
sect1.para:
📍 Location
Immediately after the header banner.
🎯 Purpose (ELI5)
Before the receptionist can work, they need their tools: a telephone (http) to talk to visitors, a ladder into the file archive (fs), a map of the building (path), and a magnifying glass to read the name tag on every request (URL).
⚙️ How It Works (Senior Depth)
All four are Node.js built-ins — this is the reason the project's only runtime dependency (dotenv, see package.json) can be treated as optional: even if node_modules were wiped, the server would still start, merely losing the polished .env parsing. URL is destructured from require("url") instead of using the global URL, which keeps the file explicit and works identically on old Node versions where the global was not yet exposed.
🔗 Trace Downward
http powers http.createServer and server.listen at the bottom.
fs powers fs.readFile in serveSPA/serveStatic and fs.createReadStream in streamDownload.
path powers every safe-path helper (isInsideRoot, serveStatic, serveSPA, streamDownload's extension lookup).
URL powers the request parsing inside the main handler.
🤝 Trace Sideways
The frontend equivalent of "requires" are the ordered <script defer> tags in index.html; the same "standard library first" spirit appears in lib/load-env.js and lib/files-service.js, which also open with plain built-in requires and no third-party imports.
💻 Actual Code
consthttp=require("http"); constfs=require("fs"); constpath=require("path"); const{URL}=require("url");
⚠️ Breaking Change Warning If you swap require("fs") for fs/promises here, the four callback-style fs.readFile(..., (err, data) => ...) call sites stop working silently at runtime (they would receive a Promise, never the buffer). Both lib/ modules already use promises, but this file intentionally does not.

sect1.title: 🧩 Block: PROJECT_ROOT and Environment Bootstrap
sect1.para:
📍 Location
Right after the requires.
🎯 Purpose (ELI5)
This is the receptionist pinning the building map on the wall. PROJECT_ROOT says "everything I serve lives here", and loadEnv pastes the office rulebook (.env) onto the wall so every later decision — which port, where the downloads live — can read it.
⚙️ How It Works (Senior Depth)
__dirname is the directory containing server.js, i.e. the repository root in this project's layout. loadEnv(PROJECT_ROOT) therefore resolves <project root>/.env. The call happens synchronously at module top level, before files-service is required — this ordering is load-bearing: PORT below and FILES_ROOT (read lazily by lib/files-service.js) both assume process.env is already populated. loadEnv prefers the dotenv package and silently falls back to a hand-rolled parser if it is not installed, and it never overwrites an existing environment variable.
📥 Inputs
File on disk: .env (template: .env.example — keys PORT, FILES_ROOT).
📤 Outputs
Populated process.env.PORT and process.env.FILES_ROOT for the whole Node process.
PROJECT_ROOT constant used by every API handler and passed as the first argument to every lib/files-service.js call.
🔗 Trace Downward
Depends on lib/load-env.js → loadEnv(), which depends on the dotenv package (optional) and fs/path.
Depends on node_modules/dotenv being installed (it is declared in package.json).
🔗 Trace Upward
.env.example documents the two keys this bootstrap makes real; DevOps copy it to .env on deploy.
nginx.conf deliberately does not configure FILES_ROOT — its comment says "FILES_ROOT is configured in the Node process .env — not in this file", i.e. this bootstrap is the single source of truth.
package.json's "start": "node server.js" is the command that triggers this whole sequence.
🤝 Trace Sideways
The "pass `PROJECT_ROOT` into the service" convention is the reason lib/files-service.js can stay testable and location-agnostic: every exported function there (listCategories, listPath, getDownloadTarget, searchEntries, listLatestReleases, peekRootSync) takes projectRoot as its first parameter instead of importing a global.
💻 Actual Code
constPROJECT_ROOT=__dirname; const{loadEnv}=require("./lib/load-env"); loadEnv(PROJECT_ROOT);
constfilesService=require("./lib/files-service");
⚠️ Breaking Change Warning Reordering these lines — e.g. requiring lib/files-service.js before calling loadEnv — still works today only because files-service reads FILES_ROOT lazily inside each request. But if files-service ever gains top-level process.env.FILES_ROOT capture (a natural "optimisation"), that reordering would make every request 503 with FILES_ROOT_MISSING. Treat the call order here as a contract, not a style choice. Renaming PROJECT_ROOT also breaks nothing internally, but any new file that mirrors this pattern should keep the same name for greppability.

sect1.title: 🧩 Block: HOST, PORT and ROOT Constants
sect1.para:
📍 Location
Directly after the files-service require.
🎯 Purpose (ELI5)
The desk's address: which door to open (HOST), which number plate to hang on it (PORT), and a nickname for the building (ROOT).
⚙️ How It Works (Senior Depth)
HOST = "0.0.0.0" binds to all interfaces. That is what allows nginx.conf to reach this process over the loopback interface (proxy_pass http://127.0.0.1:3000;) without any socket tricks. It also means the port is reachable from the network, so the security blocklist later in the request handler is not merely theoretical.
PORT reads process.env.PORT with a 3000 fallback. Note the truthiness form: PORT=0 in .env would fall through to 3000 rather than picking a random OS port — an edge case worth knowing before "fixing" it.
ROOT = PROJECT_ROOT is an alias kept purely for readability at the call sites (isInsideRoot(ROOT, fp), path.join(ROOT, ...), path.join(ROOT, "index.html")).
📥 Inputs
process.env.PORT (set by the .env bootstrap above; documented in .env.example as "HTTP port for the Node.js server").
📤 Outputs
The listen target used by server.listen(PORT, HOST, ...).
The http://localhost:${PORT} base used by decodePathname and by the new URL(req.url, ...) parsing in the main handler.
🔗 Trace Upward
nginx.conf hardcodes the expectation of this port in proxy_pass http://127.0.0.1:3000. Changing the default 3000 here without editing nginx.conf (or setting PORT in .env to match) silently 502s the whole production site.
🤝 Trace Sideways
PORT also appears in lib/load-env.js's domain (via .env) and in the printed URLs of the startup banner. The frontend never needs to know it: every fetch in assets/js/services/resource-service.js uses relative URLs ("/api/categories"), which is exactly what makes the nginx proxy transparent.
💻 Actual Code
constHOST="0.0.0.0"; constPORT=process.env.PORT||3000; constROOT=PROJECT_ROOT;
⚠️ Breaking Change Warning Changing HOST to "127.0.0.1" for "safety" is a behaviour change: in container deployments that port-map the service, health checks and the nginx upstream must both agree with the new bind address. Changing the default port breaks nginx.conf (see above) and the instructions printed in the startup banner.

sect1.title: 🧩 Block: The ANSI Colour Palette c
sect1.para:
📍 Location
After the host/port constants.
🎯 Purpose (ELI5)
A box of highlighter pens for the terminal. Each pen is a tiny invisible code that makes the next text a colour, and reset is the cap that stops the colour bleeding onto everything after it.
⚙️ How It Works (Senior Depth)
Plain string map of ANSI escape sequences — no chalk, no dependency. The keys are used in exactly three places: log() (status colouring), and the startup banner + SIGINT handler (cyan/yellow/green emphasis). Because these are raw escapes, they are emitted even when stdout is a redirected file or pipe; ANSI-aware log shippers ignore them, and non-ANSI consumers see a few harmless control characters.
📥 Inputs
None — a constant.
📤 Outputs
Colour-wrapped fragments interpolated into template literals in log(), server.listen's banner, and the shutdown message.
🤝 Trace Sideways
Dependency-free "small utility" is a house pattern: lib/load-env.js hand-rolls .env parsing for the same reason. The palette has no counterpart on the frontend — browser logs there are uncoloured.
💻 Actual Code
constc={ reset:"\x1b[0m", dim:"\x1b[2m", green:"\x1b[32m", yellow:"\x1b[33m", cyan:"\x1b[36m", red:"\x1b[31m", magenta:"\x1b[35m", bold:"\x1b[1m", };
⚠️ Breaking Change Warning Deleting an unused-looking key (magenta is currently referenced by no call site, but dim, bold, green, yellow, cyan and red all are) is safe today only if you re-check log() and the banner after any refactor. If c itself is removed, log() and server.listen throw ReferenceError: c is not defined on the first request — taking down the server exactly when it starts receiving traffic.

sect1.title: 🧩 Block: The MIME Table MIMES
sect1.para:
📍 Location
After the colour palette.
🎯 Purpose (ELI5)
This is the sticker machine at the shipping counter. Every file that leaves the building gets a sticker saying what it is — a picture, a web page, a zip — so the receiver's browser knows whether to display it, play it, or offer a download.
⚙️ How It Works (Senior Depth)
An extension → Content-Type map consulted in three places:
serveStatic — picks the header for static assets (MIMES[ext] || "application/octet-stream").
streamDownload — same fallback for downloads, so a .iso arrives as application/octet-stream and a .pdf as application/pdf even though Content-Disposition: attachment forces the save dialog anyway.
The SPA route — the odd one out: if (ext && MIMES[ext] && ext !== ".html") uses the table as an extension whitelist to decide whether a /browse/...-style path is a real asset (serve statically) or a client route (serve the SPA shell). Text entries carry charset=utf-8; binary entries deliberately do not. Note the table doubles as the project's "supported download catalogue": .iso, .qcow2, .vmdk, .docx, .vsdx are here because this portal distributes VM images and Office/Visio documents.
📥 Inputs
None — a constant.
📤 Outputs
Content-Type header values for every static and download response; an extension-membership test for the SPA-vs-static routing decision.
🔗 Trace Upward
The extensions listed here are the ones the frontend will happily link to: assets/js/router.js keeps its own fileExtensions regex (html, zip, tar, gz, iso, qcow2, vmdk, pdf, txt, log, sql, docx, xlsx, pptx, png, jpg, exec, sh, yml, yaml, md, json, csv) to decide which links must not be SPA-navigated but downloaded/navigated natively. The two lists overlap on purpose but are not identical — adding a new extension here (e.g. .deb) makes the server serve it correctly, while adding it to router.js's regex is what stops the SPA from hijacking clicks on such links.
🔗 Trace Downward
serveStatic also uses ext to pick the cache policy (no-cache for .html, public, max-age=3600 for everything else) and to decide whether a missing file should become the inline SVG placeholder (images list) or the SPA fallback (.html / extensionless).
🤝 Trace Sideways
The same "map instead of library" minimalism as the c palette. The frontend mirrors the pattern conceptually with inferIcon() in assets/js/services/resource-service.js, which maps filename patterns to icon categories.
💻 Actual Code
constMIMES={ ".html":"text/html;charset=utf-8", ".css":"text/css;charset=utf-8", ".js":"text/javascript;charset=utf-8", ".mjs":"text/javascript;charset=utf-8", ".json":"application/json;charset=utf-8", ".png":"image/png", ".jpg":"image/jpeg", ".jpeg":"image/jpeg", ".webp":"image/webp", ".svg":"image/svg+xml", ".ico":"image/x-icon", ".woff":"font/woff", ".woff2":"font/woff2", ".ttf":"font/ttf", ".map":"application/json", ".txt":"text/plain;charset=utf-8", ".pdf":"application/pdf", ".iso":"application/octet-stream", ".zip":"application/zip", ".gz":"application/gzip", ".qcow2":"application/octet-stream", ".vmdk":"application/octet-stream", ".sql":"application/sql", ".log":"text/plain;charset=utf-8", ".yml":"text/yaml;charset=utf-8", ".yaml":"text/yaml;charset=utf-8", ".sh":"text/x-shellscript", ".md":"text/markdown;charset=utf-8", ".docx":"application/vnd.openxmlformats-officedocument.wordprocessingml.document", ".vsdx":"application/vnd.ms-visio.drawing", };
⚠️ Breaking Change Warning This table is consumed by serveStatic, streamDownload and the SPA route guard. Adding an entry is additive and safe. Removing or renaming an entry silently changes behaviour in three places at once: e.g. deleting ".svg" makes SVG assets download as octet-streams and makes /browse/logo.svg fall through to the SPA shell instead of the static handler. Keep it in sync with the fileExtensions regex in assets/js/router.js and the image-extension list inside serveStatic.

assets/js/router.js
assets/js/services/resource-service.js
nginx.conf

sect1.title: 🧩 Function: log(method, status, url, extra)
sect1.para:
📍 Location
Between the MIME table and sendJSON.
🎯 Purpose (ELI5)
After every visitor interaction, the receptionist writes one line in the day-book: time, what they asked, and how it went — written in green when everything went fine, yellow when something was their mistake, red when the building itself is on fire.
⚙️ How It Works (Senior Depth)
Picks a colour from the c palette by status band (≥500 red, ≥400 yellow, ≥300 cyan, else green), timestamps with a HH:MM:SS slice of the ISO date, and pads the method to 6 characters with padEnd(6) so columns line up. Called from every terminal branch of the request handler and from the blocklist guard, always after the response has been produced, so a logging bug can never corrupt a response.
📥 Inputs
method — e.g. "GET", "HEAD".
status — numeric HTTP status.
url — the decoded pathname.
extra — optional suffix: latency (${Date.now() - start}ms), item counts (${categories.length} categories · …), service error codes.
📤 Outputs
One console.log line per handled request. No file logging — nginx.conf disables access_log for static assets and expects the Node process's stdout to be captured by the platform service manager.
🔗 Trace Upward
Consumed exclusively inside this file by the main request handler, the blocklist branch, and every API/SPA/static branch (always with the Date.now() - start latency suffix).
🤝 Trace Sideways
The frontend has a different observability culture: assets/js/services/ performance-monitor.js measures client-side performance instead. Server latency strings here ("… · 3ms") are the human-readable counterpart of the Cache-Control: no-store headers the API sends — together they say "the data is fresh and fast".
💻 Actual Code
functionlog(method,status,url,extra=""){ constcolor= status>=500?c.red: status>=400?c.yellow: status>=300?c.cyan: c.green; consttime=newDate().toISOString().slice(11,19); console.log( `${c.dim}${time}${c.reset}${c.bold}${method.padEnd(6)}${c.reset}${color}${status}${c.reset}${url}${c.dim}${extra}${c.reset}` ); }
⚠️ Breaking Change Warning Change the signature and every call site in this file must change too. Change the format and anything tailing stdout (log shippers, journalctl filters, alerting regexes on status codes) loses its anchors. Do not route log() through anything that can throw synchronously — it runs inside the request handler's try, so a throwing logger would convert successful responses into the 500 path of sendServiceError.

sect1.title: 🧩 Function: sendJSON(res, status, data, headers)
sect1.para:
📍 Location
After log.
🎯 Purpose (ELI5)
The standard envelope the receptionist puts answers in: a clean white envelope (JSON), the right stamp (Content-Type), the exact weight (Content-Length), and a sticker saying "anyone may open this" (Access-Control-Allow-Origin: *).
⚙️ How It Works (Senior Depth)
Serialises with JSON.stringify(data, null, 0) (compact), writes a header set with sensible API defaults, then spreads the caller's headers last so a call site can override any default. Every API handler in the main router funnels through this function; sendServiceError uses it too, which is how error payloads inherit the same CORS/caching policy as successes. Content-Length is computed with Buffer.byteLength(body) — correct for multi-byte UTF-8 payloads (e.g. non-ASCII filenames in search results), which body.length would get wrong.
📥 Inputs
res — the ServerResponse.
status — HTTP status code.
data — any JSON-serialisable value (arrays for listings, objects for health/errors).
headers — optional per-call overrides (currently unused by call sites, kept for future needs).
📤 Outputs
Default headers written: "Content-Type": "application/json; charset=utf-8", "Content-Length", "Access-Control-Allow-Origin": "*", "Access-Control-Allow-Methods": "GET, HEAD, OPTIONS", "Access-Control-Allow-Headers": "Content-Type", "Cache-Control": "no-store" — then the body.
🔗 Trace Upward
The most important consumer is assets/js/services/resource-service.js: its getCachedData/setCachedData implement their own 5-minute sessionStorage cache precisely because this endpoint sends Cache-Control: no-store (the HTTP cache is told never to help). Its parseError() also depends on this function's shape: res.json() is expected to yield { error: "..." } for non-OK statuses.
🔗 Trace Downward
Depends on nothing outside Node core; it is a dependency of every API branch below and of sendServiceError.
🤝 Trace Sideways
sendText is its text-bodied sibling with a reduced header set; both exist so HEAD/static/error paths never accidentally inherit the JSON content type.
💻 Actual Code
functionsendJSON(res,status,data,headers={}){ constbody=JSON.stringify(data,null,0); res.writeHead(status,{ "Content-Type":"application/json;charset=utf-8", "Content-Length":Buffer.byteLength(body), "Access-Control-Allow-Origin":"*", "Access-Control-Allow-Methods":"GET,HEAD,OPTIONS", "Access-Control-Allow-Headers":"Content-Type", "Cache-Control":"no-store", ...headers, }); res.end(body); }
⚠️ Breaking Change Warning This is the API contract writer. Narrowing Access-Control-Allow-Origin from * to a specific origin breaks any direct (non-nginx-proxied) API consumer. Removing Cache-Control: no-store turns the frontend's sessionStorage + browser-cache combination into a double cache whose invalidation you do not control. Changing the error payload shape ({ error, code }, see sendServiceError) breaks parseError() in resource-service.js and the user-visible error messages of the entire portal.

assets/js/services/resource-service.js
assets/js/home.js
assets/js/browse.js
assets/js/autocomplete.js
─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────

sect1.title: 🧩 Function: sendText(res, status, text, contentType)
sect1.para:
📍 Location
After sendJSON.

🎯 Purpose (ELI5)
The sticky-note version of an answer: short, plain text, no envelope. Used when there is nothing structured to say — "Forbidden", "404 — whatever you
   typed", "Bad Request".

⚙️ How It Works (Senior Depth)
Writes only Content-Type (defaulting to text/plain; charset=utf-8, overridable) and Access-Control-Allow-Origin: *, then the body. Note the deliberate differences from sendJSON: no Content-Length (Node uses chunked encoding), and no Cache-Control (errors are cacheable per HTTP defaults, which is acceptable for these never-changing messages).

📥 Inputs


res, status, text, optional contentType.



📤 Outputs
A plain-text response body with CORS enabled.

🔗 Trace Upward
Called from: URL-parse failure (400), method guard (405), the security blocklist (403), serveStatic (403 traversal, 404 missing asset), serveSPA (500 when index.html is missing), streamDownload (500 when the read stream errors before headers are sent). It is this file's universal "say something honest, quickly" path.

🤝 Trace Sideways
Frontend error handling rarely surfaces these raw strings: for API calls, resource-service.js's parseError() prefers the JSON {error} body from sendServiceError; for page navigation, router.js simply lets the browser display the text.

💻 Actual Code
functionsendText(res,status,text,contentType="text/plain;charset=utf-8"){
res.writeHead(status,{
"Content-Type":contentType,
"Access-Control-Allow-Origin":"*",
});
res.end(text);
}


⚠️ Breaking Change Warning Adding Cache-Control headers here would change how browsers and upstream proxies (nginx in production) cache error responses — with a long max-age, a single transient 500 for index.html could stick at the proxy. Removing the CORS header breaks browser-visible error text for cross-origin API consumers. Keep this function boring; it is the last line of defence when everything else has already gone wrong.

sect1.title: 🧩 Function: sendServiceError(res, err)
sect1.para:
📍 Location
After sendText.

🎯 Purpose (ELI5)
The translator between the specialists in the back office and the visitor. When a specialist hands the receptionist a slip saying "this shelf does not
   exist" or "you may not go in there", this turns the slip into a proper, polite JSON answer with the right number on it.

⚙️ How It Works (Senior Depth)
Reads two duck-typed properties that lib/files-service.js's serviceError() attaches to plain Error objects: err.httpStatus (default 500) and err.code (default "INTERNAL"). Responds with { error: err.message || "Unexpected error", code: err.code || "INTERNAL" }. The || defaults make the function safe for unexpected errors (a real TypeError, an fs error without annotations) as well as expected service errors — this is the single convergence point of the main handler's catch (err).

📥 Inputs


err — any thrown value; service errors from lib/files-service.js carry { httpStatus, code, message }.



📤 Outputs
Via sendJSON: e.g. 503 { "error": "FILES_ROOT does not exist…", "code": "FILES_ROOT_NOT_FOUND" } or 403 { "error": "Requested path is outside FILES_ROOT.", "code": "PATH_TRAVERSAL" }.

🔗 Trace Upward


assets/js/services/resource-service.js → parseError(res) reads body.error and throws it as a JS Error message; that message is ultimately displayed to users by home.js and browse.js in their error cards.

The code values (FILES_ROOT_MISSING, FILES_ROOT_NOT_FOUND, FILES_ROOT_NOT_DIRECTORY, FILES_ROOT_EMPTY, FILES_ROOT_NO_CATEGORIES, INVALID_PATH, PATH_TRAVERSAL, NOT_FOUND, NOT_A_DIRECTORY, NOT_A_FILE) are defined in lib/files-service.js and are also echoed into the request log line via err.code || err.message.

The health endpoint complements this: instead of raising these errors it reports the FILES_ROOT state as "degraded" via peekRootSync, so uptime monitors can alert before users see the errors.



🤝 Trace Sideways
This is the same "transport maps domain errors to HTTP" pattern used by every serious Node codebase; here it is 6 lines because the domain layer already annotates its errors. Nothing in the frontend distinguishes error from code today except display — but code is the stable machine-readable field for future logic.

💻 Actual Code
functionsendServiceError(res,err){
conststatus=err.httpStatus||500;
sendJSON(res,status,{
error:err.message||"Unexpectederror",
code:err.code||"INTERNAL",
});
}


⚠️ Breaking Change Warning The property names httpStatus and code are a cross-file contract with lib/files-service.js's serviceError(). Renaming either side breaks error handling invisibly — every domain error would become a generic 500 INTERNAL while tests using only success paths stay green. Changing the JSON keys (error, code) breaks parseError() in resource-service.js and therefore every error message the UI shows.

sect1.title: 🧩 Function: securityHeaders(res)
sect1.para:
📍 Location
After sendServiceError.

🎯 Purpose (ELI5)
Three safety stickers glued onto every page and asset leaving the building: "don't guess what I am" (nosniff), "you may frame me only from my own
   house" (SAMEORIGIN), and "when people mention where they came from, be
   discreet" (referrer policy).

⚙️ How It Works (Senior Depth)
Uses res.setHeader (merge-patch semantics, applied before res.writeHead) rather than passing headers to writeHead, so it can be composed with any later writeHead without collision. Called by serveSPA (both success and via serveStatic's fallback) and by the success path of serveStatic. It is intentionally not called by streamDownload, which sets its own strict subset (X-Content-Type-Options inline) — a download is never framed or navigated, only saved.

📥 Inputs


res — the ServerResponse.



📤 Outputs
Response headers: X-Content-Type-Options: nosniff, X-Frame-Options: SAMEORIGIN, Referrer-Policy: strict-origin-when-cross-origin.

🔗 Trace Upward
nginx.conf adds the same three headers (plus HSTS and X-XSS-Protection) with add_header ... always at the server level. Caution is warranted: nginx's add_header inheritance rules mean the location /api/ and static-asset blocks (which declare their own add_header) do not inherit the server-level set — so this function is what guarantees the headers on responses served directly by Node during development, and duplicates them harmlessly for proxied API responses.

🤝 Trace Sideways
The security posture matches the frontend's: index.html pins theme/perf state before paint (see index.html's inline boot script) — the pair "strict server headers + strict pre-paint boot" is the project's defence-in-depth habit.

💻 Actual Code
functionsecurityHeaders(res){
res.setHeader("X-Content-Type-Options","nosniff");
res.setHeader("X-Frame-Options","SAMEORIGIN");
res.setHeader("Referrer-Policy","strict-origin-when-cross-origin");
}


⚠️ Breaking Change Warning Removing nosniff re-enables MIME-sniffing attacks on user-controlled content served from FILES_ROOT (the downloads tree is user-curated!). Changing SAMEORIGIN to DENY breaks any future legitimate embedding of the portal. These headers are asserted twice in the deployment (here and in nginx.conf); keep the two lists consistent or document the divergence.

sect1.title: 🧩 Function: isInsideRoot(rootDir, filePath)
sect1.para:
📍 Location
After securityHeaders.
🎯 Purpose (ELI5)
The "are you still inside the building?" checker. A visitor may wander to room 3, shelf 2 — fine. But a request for "the basement of the building across the street" (../../etc/passwd-style) must be answered with a simple no.
⚙️ How It Works (Senior Depth)
The canonical path-traversal test: path.relative(rootDir, filePath) yields "" when the paths are equal, a ../-prefixed string when the target escapes, or an absolute path on a different drive (Windows). The expression rel && !rel.startsWith("..") && !path.isAbsolute(rel) therefore accepts strictly-*inside* targets (rejecting the root itself via rel &&) — and serveStatic re-admits the one exception (index.html) explicitly with path.resolve(fp) !== path.resolve(ROOT, "index.html").
📥 Inputs
rootDir — always ROOT (the project root) in this file.
filePath — a joined candidate path under test.
📤 Outputs
Boolean. Consumed once, in serveStatic's guard, which answers 403 "Forbidden" when it fails.
🔗 Trace Downward
Depends only on Node's path module and its platform-correct separators.
🔗 Trace Upward
It protects only the static handler. The API's downloads/listings are guarded by a second, independent checker: resolveInsideRoot() in lib/files-service.js, which additionally rejects ./../NUL segments before resolving and throws a typed PATH_TRAVERSAL service error. Two checkers exist because the two layers protect different roots: this one protects the source tree (project root), that one protects the content tree (FILES_ROOT).
🤝 Trace Sideways
Defense-in-depth pairs: serveStatic also strips leading ../ sequences with path.normalize(...).replace(/^(\.\.[\/\\])+/, "") before joining, and nginx adds a third layer (location ~ /\. deny all) in production.
💻 Actual Code
functionisInsideRoot(rootDir,filePath){ constrel=path.relative(rootDir,filePath); returnrel&&!rel.startsWith("..")&&!path.isAbsolute(rel); }
⚠️ Breaking Change Warning "Simplifying" this to !rel.startsWith("..") (dropping rel &&) would make the root itself pass the check, which combined with the index.html exception in serveStatic changes which paths are servable. Loosening it at all means any static-asset request can read server.js, lib/*.js and .env-adjacent files if the blocklist is ever bypassed — it is the last pure-Node barrier in front of the source tree. Keep the double-guard (this + resolveInsideRoot) intact.

sect1.title: 🧩 Function: decodePathname(rawUrl)
sect1.para:
📍 Location
After isInsideRoot.
🎯 Purpose (ELI5)
The name-tag reader. When a visitor's badge says D9%81D8A7... (weird symbols for a Persian folder name) or my%20files, this translates it into what the folder is actually called on disk.
⚙️ How It Works (Senior Depth)
Builds a URL against a synthetic http://localhost:${PORT} base (so request targets like /api/files/x parse even without an absolute URL), takes .pathname (dropping the query string), and percent-decodes it once. In the current code it is defined but the main handler performs the equivalent parse inline — the function remains as the single, documented recipe for "pathname decoding" and as a ready-made tool for refactors; note it is referenced by neither call site today (verified by search), so treat edits here as API hygiene, not hot-path changes.
📥 Inputs
rawUrl — req.url, e.g. "/api/download/ISO%20Images/win11.iso".
📤 Outputs
A decoded pathname string, e.g. /api/download/ISO Images/win11.iso.
🔗 Trace Upward
Percent-encoded path segments come from the frontend's encodeRelPath() in assets/js/services/resource-service.js, which maps every path segment through encodeURIComponent — the two functions are the encode/decode pair that make non-ASCII filenames work end-to-end (including Persian category names, matching the portal's FA language support in assets/js/i18n.js).
🔗 Trace Downward
Depends on the global-ish URL constructor destructured in the requires and on PORT for the base URL.
💻 Actual Code
functiondecodePathname(rawUrl){ returndecodeURIComponent(newURL(rawUrl,`http://localhost:${PORT}`).pathname); }
⚠️ Breaking Change Warning Decoding is the vulnerable half of the encode/decode pair: applying it twice (or using decodeURIComponent on the whole URL including the query) would let %2e%2e%2f smuggle traversal sequences past naive filters before the guards see them. Any caller must decode before security checks and only once. If you wire this into the main handler, wrap it in the existing try — malformed sequences throw URIError and must surface as 400.

sect1.title: 🧩 Function: relFromPrefix(pathname, prefix)
sect1.para:
📍 Location
After decodePathname.

🎯 Purpose (ELI5)
The "cut here" scissors. The visitor says "/api/download/ISOs/win11.iso"; the receptionist cuts off the "/api/download" label and hands the rest — "ISOs/win11.iso" — to the specialist.

⚙️ How It Works (Senior Depth)
pathname.slice(prefix.length) removes the prefix verbatim, then replace(/^\/+/, "") strips any leading slashes so the service receives a clean relative path. Used by exactly two branches of the router: /api/files/... and /api/download/..., in their path-segment form (as opposed to their ?path= query form, which skips this helper). Note the prefix slicing relies on the decoded pathname matching the prefix byte-for-byte — spaces and Unicode are fine, but a prefix that itself contained percent-encodings would not match.

📥 Inputs


pathname — decoded pathname.

prefix — "/api/files" or "/api/download".



📤 Outputs
Relative path string (possibly "" for /api/files/ with no tail), which is passed as relPath to filesService.listPath / getDownloadTarget.

🔗 Trace Upward
The counterpart encoder is encodeRelPath() in assets/js/services/resource-service.js; links are produced there by browseHref() (→ /browse/..., SPA routes) and downloadHref() (→ /api/download/..., these endpoints) — and autocomplete.js builds <li data-href> items from the same helpers.

💻 Actual Code
functionrelFromPrefix(pathname,prefix){
constrest=pathname.slice(prefix.length);
returnrest.replace(/^\/+/,"");
}


⚠️ Breaking Change Warning This helper is what defines the URL grammar of the API. If the router's pathname.startsWith("/api/files/") branches change (e.g. you add /api/v2/files), every branch and this helper must be updated together, otherwise slice() will cut at the wrong offset and the service will receive a corrupted relPath (surfacing as 404/400 from lib/files-service.js). Frontend producers of these URLs live in resource-service.js (downloadHref, listFiles) and must be updated in the same commit.

sect1.title: 🧩 Function: contentDisposition(fileName)
sect1.para:
📍 Location
After relFromPrefix.
🎯 Purpose (ELI5)
The shipping label writer. When a big box (file download) leaves the building, this writes the recipient's name on it twice: once in simple letters everyone can read, and once in "international handwriting" so names in any language (yes, even Persian!) survive the trip.
⚙️ How It Works (Senior Depth)
Implements RFC 5987/6266 dual-encoding for Content-Disposition:
fallback — strips every character outside printable ASCII ([^\x20-\x7E] → _) and removes double quotes, producing a safe legacy filename="..." for ancient clients.
encoded — the full encodeURIComponent form for the filename*=UTF-8''... variant understood by all modern browsers, preserving Unicode (e.g. Persian) filenames exactly. Consumed only by streamDownload, which stamps it on every download response so the browser saves the file instead of trying to render it.
📥 Inputs
fileName — the basename from filesService.getDownloadTarget (the last segment of the validated relative path).
📤 Outputs
A complete header value, e.g. attachment; filename="win11_iso"; filename*=UTF-8''win11.iso.
🔗 Trace Upward
Filenames arrive from FILES_ROOT (arbitrary, user-curated names — that is the whole point of a file portal) after validation by lib/files-service.js. The attachment disposition is the third layer of download safety, alongside X-Content-Type-Options: nosniff (same header block in streamDownload) and the NOT_A_FILE type check in the service.
🔗 Trace Downward
Pure string manipulation — no dependencies beyond the JS standard library.
🤝 Trace Sideways
On the client, resource-service.js's downloadHref() builds the URL that triggers this path, and router.js's fileExtensions regex ensures the SPA's click-interceptor stands aside for file links, letting the browser's native download (and thus this header) do its job.
💻 Actual Code
functioncontentDisposition(fileName){ constfallback=String(fileName).replace(/[^\x20-\x7E]/g,"_").replace(/"/g,""); constencoded=encodeURIComponent(fileName); return`attachment;filename="${fallback}";filename*=UTF-8''${encoded}`; }
⚠️ Breaking Change Warning This is a header-injection boundary. Removing the .replace(/"/g, "") would allow a maliciously-named file (x".html"; filename*=...) to inject extra header parameters. Changing attachment to inline turns the downloads tree into a drive-by content-rendering surface (combined with MIME types from MIMES). The regex is byte-literal — keep it exactly as is unless you have a fuzz-tested replacement.

sect1.title: 🧩 Block: server.listen(PORT, HOST, …) — Startup Banner
sect1.para:
📍 Location
Immediately after http.createServer.

🎯 Purpose (ELI5)
The moment the reception desk opens, it pins a big friendly sign on the door: "we are open, here is where the rooms are, and here is whether the
   archive room actually exists today." That last bit matters — if the manager forgot to write FILES_ROOT on the rulebook, the sign turns yellow and tells you exactly what is missing instead of letting the server limp along mysteriously.

⚙️ How It Works (Senior Depth)
The callback runs once the socket is bound. It calls filesService.peekRootSync(PROJECT_ROOT) and converts the three failure dimensions into a colour-coded status line: not configured → yellow "FILES_ROOT is not set"; missing path → yellow "FILES_ROOT path was not
   found"; not a directory → yellow "FILES_ROOT is not a directory"; otherwise green "FILES_ROOT is configured". It then prints the boxed banner with all six canonical endpoint URLs. Note the deliberate choice to not exit on a bad FILES_ROOT — the server still starts, health reports "degraded", and API calls will answer typed 503s from lib/files-service.js; this makes misconfiguration observable rather than fatal, which is friendlier to container orchestration that restarts crash-looping processes.

📥 Inputs


PORT, HOST constants; FILES_ROOT (via peekRootSync reading process.env).



📤 Outputs
Stdout: the banner, the FILES_ROOT status, the hint "Set FILES_ROOT in .env — no filesystem paths are hardcoded." and "Press Ctrl+C to stop".

🔗 Trace Upward
Triggered by npm start (package.json) in dev, or by the process manager in production behind nginx.conf.

🔗 Trace Downward
Depends on filesService.peekRootSync — the only synchronous export of the service, chosen so the banner never needs async plumbing.

🤝 Trace Sideways
The banner's endpoint list is a human-readable mirror of the router: /api/health, /api/categories, /api/files/<category>, /api/download/<category>/<file>, /api/search?q=, /api/releases. The .env hint mirrors .env.example's comments verbatim in spirit.

💻 Actual Code
server.listen(PORT,HOST,()=>{
constpeek=filesService.peekRootSync(PROJECT_ROOT);
constrootState=!peek.configured
?`${c.yellow}FILES_ROOTisnotset${c.reset}`
:!peek.exists
?`${c.yellow}FILES_ROOTpathwasnotfound${c.reset}`
:!peek.isDirectory
?`${c.yellow}FILES_ROOTisnotadirectory${c.reset}`
:`${c.green}FILES_ROOTisconfigured${c.reset}`;

console.log(`
${c.cyan}${c.bold}
╔══════════════════════════════════════════════════╗
║CloudAvidFilePortal—FileAPIServer║
╚══════════════════════════════════════════════════╝${c.reset}

${c.green}➜${c.reset}Local:${c.bold}http://localhost:${PORT}/${c.reset}
${c.green}➜${c.reset}Health:http://localhost:${PORT}/api/health
${c.green}➜${c.reset}Categories:http://localhost:${PORT}/api/categories
${c.green}➜${c.reset}Files:http://localhost:${PORT}/api/files/<category>
${c.green}➜${c.reset}Download:http://localhost:${PORT}/api/download/<category>/<file>
${c.green}➜${c.reset}Search:http://localhost:${PORT}/api/search?q=
${c.green}➜${c.reset}Releases:http://localhost:${PORT}/api/releases

${rootState}
${c.dim}SetFILES_ROOTin.env—nofilesystempathsarehardcoded.${c.reset}
${c.dim}PressCtrl+Ctostop${c.reset}
`);
});


⚠️ Breaking Change Warning Anything parsing this banner (container startup probes grepping for "configured", documentation screenshots, onboarding scripts) breaks on wording changes. More subtly: peekRootSync runs once, at startup — if FILES_ROOT becomes valid after boot (a volume mount arriving late in containers), the banner stays yellow while requests succeed. Do not "fix" that by making the server exit on a bad root; the current start-anyway + degraded-health behaviour is the intended contract.

sect1.title: 🧩 Block: The SIGINT Shutdown Handler
sect1.para:
📍 Location
The final statement of server.js.

🎯 Purpose (ELI5)
The closing-time ritual. When the operator presses Ctrl+C, the receptionist doesn't just run out the door mid-sentence — they finish the sentence, politely say "Shutting down file portal…", lock the door, and then turn off the lights.

⚙️ How It Works (Senior Depth)
process.on("SIGINT", …) intercepts Ctrl+C (and the SIGINT signal sent by container stop sequences), prints a yellow notice, and calls server.close(() => process.exit(0)). server.close stops accepting new connections but lets in-flight requests (notably active streamDownload pipes!) finish before the callback fires and exits with code 0. Edge case worth knowing: if a download is streaming and the client never disconnects, close's callback can be delayed indefinitely — that is precisely why streamDownload registers req.on("close") to destroy streams on client disconnects, and why an operator may still need a second Ctrl+C (which, with this handler installed, is captured again and merely re-runs the same path) or a SIGKILL from the orchestrator.

📥 Inputs


The OS signal SIGINT.



📤 Outputs
Stdout notice; process exit code 0 after graceful drain.

🔗 Trace Upward
Depended upon by deployment hygiene: nginx.conf's 3600s proxy timeouts imply long-lived download connections, and graceful drain is what makes systemctl restart-style operations not truncate user downloads.

🔗 Trace Downward
Depends on server (the http.Server instance) and console.

🤝 Trace Sideways
The frontend has no equivalent — browsers own their lifecycle. The closest analogue is resource-service.js's clearCache(), another explicit "clean up before leaving" utility.

💻 Actual Code
process.on("SIGINT",()=>{
console.log(`\n${c.yellow}Shuttingdownfileportal…${c.reset}`);
server.close(()=>process.exit(0));
});


⚠️ Breaking Change Warning Removing this handler reverts Ctrl+C to Node's default: immediate termination, truncated streams, and the nginx.conf upstream briefly serving connection-refused 502s during every restart. Replacing process.exit(0) with a nonzero code can make orchestrators treat planned restarts as crashes. If you later add SIGTERM support (recommended for containers), reuse this same close-and-exit body — two divergent shutdown paths is how zombie downloads happen.
